slides: Open by separating affine location from vector measurement. Students often bring a hidden origin into every problem, so make the first move conceptual: the chapter studies points first, then differences of points, and only then lengths, angles, rigid motions, compact-set distances, and symmetrization.

Use this map to prevent the lecture from feeling like five unrelated topics. The common test is always the same: identify what object is being moved or compared, identify the measurement attached to it, and name the invariant that survives the construction.

Spend time on the grammar of the formula rather than racing to computations. P and Q are points, Q minus P is a vector, and the norm is applied only after subtraction. This slide is the place to correct the quiet habit of treating every point as already a vector from the origin.

Emphasize that the coordinate expression is a diagnostic, not the definition of the geometry. The linear part controls metric preservation, while the translation only changes placement. The determinant and the fixed-set equation then become compact tests for the four plane motion types.

Make the classification feel earned from invariants rather than memorized from pictures. Every panel preserves internal distances, so the difference among the motions comes from orientation and fixed-set behavior. Ask students which checks would fail if a tiny anisotropic scale were hidden inside the matrix.

Use this slide as the algebraic bridge into reflection geometry. The formula H equals two u u transpose minus I is short, but it carries three important facts: lengths are preserved, applying the reflection twice returns the starting vector, and orientation changes sign.

Frame the billiard construction as a proof technique rather than a simulation trick. The folded path is locally governed by equal-angle reflection, while the unfolded path reveals the global straight line. Students should inspect how reversing the normal component is the same operation in both views.

Slow down on the two directed distances. Hausdorff distance is not asking for one closest pair; it asks whether every point of each compact set lies near the other set. The worse directed witness supplies the symmetric distance and explains the maximum in the formula.

Use the threshold view to make the supremum operational. At small epsilon, only part of each sample is covered by the opposite neighborhood. At the Hausdorff value, both directed coverage fractions finally reach one, so the metric becomes a containment certificate.

Present Steiner symmetrization as a fiberwise operation, not as a vague smoothing process. Each vertical slice keeps its one-dimensional length but is recentered about the symmetry axis. Area is preserved because the fibers keep their lengths, while perimeter and shape can change noticeably.

This diagnostic slide is useful because visual plausibility is not enough for Euclidean rigidity. The near motion looks close to a rotation and translation, but A.T A is not the identity and pairwise distances drift. The chapter's computational habit is to reject such motions by invariant checks.

Close by tying the chapter back to a reusable reading practice. In Euclidean affine geometry, every picture should answer three questions: what are the points, what vectors or set distances are being measured, and which invariant certifies the claimed construction or theorem.
